metadata.title: Hamilton says Vance’s attacks on his religion are ‘really sad,’ ‘pathetic’

sources.news_title: Kansas Senate candidate Hamilton says Vance misrepresented his faith
sources.text:
Democratic Kansas Senate candidate Adam Hamilton accused Vice President JD Vance of attacking his faith and spreading falsehoods about his religious beliefs, as Republicans battle to protect a seat they have held for more than a century in what has become one of the most closely watched races of the 2026 midterm elections.
Hamilton, the pastor of the Church of the Resurrection, the nation's largest United Methodist congregation, responded during an interview that aired Sunday on ABC News' This Week after Vance questioned his Christian beliefs and accused him of holding views that were inconsistent with Christianity. During the interview, host Jonathan Karl referenced remarks in which Vance said Hamilton believed "it's a sin to be white and a sin to raise cattle and eat meat."
"I thought it was a sign of desperation," Hamilton said. "It was pathetic. He doesn't know me. Doesn't know anything about my faith."
The clash comes as Democrats look to pull off a historic upset in Kansas. Republicans have held the Senate seat continuously since 1919, and no Democrat has won a Kansas Senate election since George McGill's reelection in 1932. Yet recent polling from Wedgewood Polls has suggested the race between Republican Senator Roger Marshall and Hamilton is effectively tied, prompting national Republicans to devote increasing attention to Kansas, a state President Donald Trump carried by more than 16 points in 2024.
Hamilton has emerged as an unconventional Democratic challenger. A longtime pastor and author of more than 30 books on Christianity and theology, he has campaigned as a centrist focused on affordability, energy costs, healthcare and agriculture while seeking support from independents and moderate Republicans.
Newsweek reached out to Vance, Marshall, and Hamilton on Sunday for comments.
Hamilton Pushes Back on Vance's Remarks
During Sunday's interview, Karl asked Hamilton about remarks Vance, who is Catholic, made during a September 14 campaign stop in Olathe, Kansas, while campaigning for Marshall.
Hamilton said he was surprised by the attack.
"The vice president of the United States would come here and attack the faith of a pastor of the largest church in the state of Kansas, the largest United Methodist church in the country," he said.
Hamilton pointed to his decades in ministry and challenged Vance's characterization of his beliefs.
"I wake up every morning. I slip to my knees. I offer my life to Christ. I pray for the Holy Spirit to lead me. I read scripture. I carry the Bible with me everywhere I go," he said.
At one point, Hamilton added: "Let's compare theology. Let's compare our faith and the impact we're having on the world."
'Every Single Line...Was a Lie'
Karl also cited comments in which Vance accused Hamilton of holding views that he argued were inconsistent with Christianity.
According to the remarks read on-air, Vance said Hamilton believes "it's a sin to be white and a sin to raise cattle and eat meat."
Hamilton flatly rejected the accusation.
"Every single line of what you just read was a lie," he said. "There was no part of what he said was true."
Hamilton said the criticism stemmed from a sermon discussing racism and the Christian concept of repentance.
"I never talked about repenting for being white. You can't find that in anything I've ever said. Or repenting for eating beef," he said.
He argued the controversy reflected broader problems in the country's political discourse.
"That's what's wrong with our country today, with our politics, with what's happening in Washington, D.C.," Hamilton said.
A Different Kind of Kansas Democrat
The exchange highlights why Republicans have targeted Hamilton aggressively in recent weeks.
Marshall and his allies have attempted to portray Hamilton as a liberal Democrat out of step with Kansas voters. Marshall has previously described him as "too woke for Kansas," while Republicans have argued his sermons mirror the national Democratic Party's priorities.
Marshall's campaign also accused Hamilton of mishandling allegations involving a church camp worker accused of sexually abusing minors.
In a statement to Newsweek on Sunday, Marshall's campaign sharply criticized Hamilton, saying: "Kansans have a clear choice this election: a senator who has fought for and delivered major wins for our farmers, cut taxes for the middle class, and secured the border, or a Chuck Schumer-funded Democrat who protected and enabled a pedophile preying on children at his church camp by refusing to report him to the police and welcoming him back to the camp to harm more children."
The statement reflects a broader Republican effort to paint Hamilton as a liberal candidate whose views are out of step with Kansas voters.
Hamilton has instead tried to present himself as a faith-based moderate. During Sunday's interview on This Week, he emphasized that he spent much of his life as a Republican and said he has supported candidates from both parties.
In a recent Politico interview, Hamilton described himself as "an independent-minded Democrat."
"I'm standing in the center, and it's the extremes that seem to be trying to pull us apart," he said. "But I think there's far more of us who stand in the center saying, look, we've got to work together."
Hamilton's balancing act reflects a broader challenge facing Democrats in red states. Earlier this month, Hamilton suggested former Vice President Kamala Harris should keep her distance from the Kansas race, arguing her involvement could undermine his ability to win over crossover voters in a state Trump carried comfortably in 2024.
The comment underscored Hamilton's effort to position himself as an independent-minded candidate rather than a standard national Democrat, a theme he returned to repeatedly during Sunday's interview. Hamilton said he had been both a Republican and a Democrat during his adult life and argued that voters were looking for leaders focused on competence and character rather than party labels.
"What matters to me more than the letter behind your name is who you are, what you stand for, your character," he said.
Why Kansas Matters
The increasingly heated rhetoric underscores growing Republican concerns about a race that, until recently, was not expected to be competitive.
National forecasters have steadily moved Kansas closer to battleground status as Democrats seek the four-seat net gain needed to retake control of the Senate. Concerns about inflation, diesel and fertilizer costs, the war in Iran and Trump's approval ratings have helped put pressure on Republicans in several red and red-leaning states.
Hamilton has particularly focused on economic frustrations among farmers and rural communities, arguing that Republicans have failed to address rising costs.
On Sunday, he said many Kansans who supported Trump now feel Washington is not listening to them.
"We need a senator who's going to say, Mr. President, this is not good for my people," Hamilton said.
Whether that message is enough to break one of the longest Senate winning streaks in American politics remains to be seen. The Cook Political Report recently moved the race from "Leans Republican" to "Toss Up."

Pastor Slams Vance’s ‘Pathetic’ Attack on His Faith
sources.text:
Pastor Slams Vance’s ‘Pathetic’ Attack on His Faith
The Democratic nominee challenged the VP to “compare our faith and the impact we’re having on the world.”
United Methodist Church pastor Adam Hamilton has condemned JD Vance’s wild smears against him.
Reverend Hamilton, 62, who is running for Senate in Kansas, appeared on ABC’s This Week with Jonathan Karl on Sunday, following Vance’s claims at a Kansas rally last month that the Democratic minister would “insult your faith and spit on your religion to accrue donations to himself.”
“He really went after you,” Karl summarized, with Hamilton agreeing: “He did.”
Karl noted: “I mean, he called your views ‘left wing radicalism dressed in the skin suit of our religion.’ Saying of your religion, of you and your beliefs, ‘that is not Christianity.’”
Asked his opinion on Vance’s fighting words, Hamilton judged: “Well, I thought it was a sign of desperation. And I thought it was really sad, it was pathetic.

“He doesn’t know me, doesn’t know anything about my faith. He came in attacking—you know, when did we start attacking people’s faith?”
Hamilton, who initially considered running as an Independent and serves a congregation of mixed political allegiances, went on to describe his dedication to his faith before taking a hit at Vance’s more hardline form of Christian values.
“I not only seek to be a follower of Jesus but to practice that in how I treat other people,” he said. “And I just would say, examine my life, examine the way I’ve tried to live, and then I want to see Mr. Vice President.
“Let’s compare. Let’s compare theology, let’s compare our faith and the impact we’re having on the world. And I just—I don’t even want to compare myself to him—I just want to say I’m doing the best I can as a follower of Jesus Christ every day.”
The author of dozens of religious books concluded: “I thought it was a sad statement that the vice president of the United States would come here and attack the faith of the pastor of the largest church in the state of Kansas, the largest United Methodist church in the country.”
While 42-year-old Vance was more than happy to throw barbs at someone else’s faith, his own take on Christianity has frequently been called into question.
Vance converted to Catholicism in 2019 at the age of 35, and—between bouts of feuding with the Pope—admitted last year that he wasn’t fully studied up on the Catechism quite yet.
Speaking at the National Catholic Prayer Breakfast, he shared: “I recognize very much that I am a baby Catholic… If you ever hear me pontificating about the Catholic faith, please recognize it comes from a place of deep belief, but it also comes from a place of not always knowing everything all the time.”

sources.text:
Did anyone think that red-state Kansas would be a political hotbed during the 2026 midterm election?
PoliticusUSA is 100% independent news and opinion. Please support us by becoming a subscriber.
The fact that Kansas is in play for Democrats, not just in the Senate election but also in House races and state races, is due to the level of economic damage, hardship, and pain that Donald Trump and his policies have brought down upon the Midwest.
In a normal midterm election where the out of power party is expected to do well, the Kansas US Senate race would not be expected to be closely contested.
Republicans are so worried about Kansas that they sent Vice President JD Vance to the state to campaign. When Vance was in Kansas, he drew a small crowd and got heckled, which revealed a lot about the mood toward Trump and Republicans in the state.
ABC This Week’s Jon Karl said to Hamilton, “The vice president came to campaign against you.”
Hamilton responded, “ I consider that a great compliment, that the second most powerful man in America came here to try to save Roger Marshall.”
It was when Hamilton was asked about Vance’s attacks on his religion that the Kansas Democrat destroyed the VP.

sources.news_title: Hamilton Slams Vance's 'Skin Suit' Jab: Attacking Someone's Faith Is 'Sad'
sources.text:
Jonathan Karl interviewed Senate candidate Adam Hamilton this morning on ABC's This Week.
Watch the interview above, and you'll understand why this Democrat is polling ahead of Republican incumbent Roger Marshall in Kansas. Republicans are freaking out about Hamilton flipping the Kansas Senate seat blue. Trump sent J.D. Vance to Kansas City last week to campaign for Roger Marshall. The Vice President told the audience that Hamilton stood for "left-wing radicalism dressed in the skin suit of our religion" and said his liberal stance on issues was not Christian.
When Karl asked Hamilton about Vance's comments, here's how he responded:
"I thought it was really sad. It was pathetic. He doesn't know anything about me. When did we start attacking people's faith? I thought it was a sad statement that the VP would come here and attack the faith of the pastor of the largest church in the state of Kansas."
In the interview, Karl played a clip of the U.S. Vice President attacking the pastor. Vance said that Hamilton thought it was a sin to be white, to raise cattle and eat meat. The Vice President claimed the Senate candidate supported groups that "spit on God-fearing Americans and mock everything that we hold dear."
In other words, Vance believes he and Trump get to pick which Christians count? I never read THAT in the Bible.
The United Methodist pastor replied calmly but firmly:
"Yes, so every single line of what you just read was a lie. It was a falsehood. It was like 180 degrees different from the reality. So, there was no part of what he said was true. And, I, you know, I find it interesting.
No, it’s not a sin to raise cattle and eat meat. So, there was a sermon that I talked about: repenting is changing the way you think about things...And I talked about racism. And in the context of racism, you know, part of what you’re trying to do is see the world through somebody else’s eyes. I never talked about repenting for being white. You can’t find that in anything I’ve ever said. Or repenting for eating beef."
Hamilton said Vice President Vance’s attacks on his religion show what is wrong in our country and are one of the reasons he is running for office. He told Karl that he is not going to Washington to “be the chaplain of the Senate or to somehow force my religion on other people.” He wants to serve in the Senate to protect the Constitution and everyone's rights.

sources.news_title: Vance Called a Pastor’s Faith a ‘Skin Suit.’ The Pastor Fired Back. - The Hip Hop Democrat
sources.text:
When the Vice President of the United States calls your Christianity a costume, you know the playbook is getting desperate.
Kansas Senate candidate Adam Hamilton, the founding pastor of the Church of the Resurrection (the largest United Methodist congregation in America), clapped back at JD Vance this week after the VP launched a pointed attack on Hamilton’s religious beliefs at a rally for Republican incumbent Roger Marshall.
What Vance Said
At a Kansas campaign rally, Vance took aim at Hamilton’s church for sponsoring Kansas City Pridefest. He claimed Hamilton was “supporting groups that spit on God-fearing Americans and mock everything that we hold dear,” according to multiple reports. Then Vance went further, calling Hamilton’s faith “not Christianity” but “left-wing radicalism dressed in the skin suit of our religion.”
Read that again. The Vice President told a lifelong pastor that his faith is a disguise.
Hamilton’s Response
In an interview with ABC’s Jonathan Karl, Hamilton called Vance’s attacks “really sad” and “pathetic,” The Hill reported. “He doesn’t know me, doesn’t know anything about my faith,” Hamilton said. He also framed the attacks as a sign of desperation, asking plainly: “When do we start attacking people’s faith?”
Hamilton is no fringe candidate. He raised a record $3.66 million in his first two months, per KCTV5, the biggest launch haul in Kansas Senate history. He won the Democratic primary in August and is running on a platform of decency, social safety nets, and church-state separation. If he wins, he would be Kansas’ first Democratic senator since 1932, Forbes noted.
Why This Matters
This is bigger than one Senate race. For years, conservative politicians have acted like they hold a monopoly on faith. Vance’s attack exposes that assumption for what it is: a political weapon, not a spiritual conviction. When a pastor who built the largest Methodist church in the country gets told his Christianity is fake because he sponsored a Pride event, the message is clear. In this version of politics, faith only counts if it excludes.
Hip-hop has always challenged gatekeepers. From Chance the Rapper weaving gospel into “Coloring Book” to Kendrick Lamar wrestling with faith on “DAMN.,” the culture understands that spirituality is personal, complex, and nobody’s to police. Hamilton may not be from hip-hop, but the principle is the same: nobody gets to tell you your belief isn’t real because it looks different from theirs.
The Takeaway
When your opponent’s best move is attacking your faith instead of your policy, that tells you everything about who is running out of ideas. Kansas voters have a real choice in November. Pay attention.
